text: Not every interesting paper is a reasonable reproduction target. Picking well here saves you from the single most common failure mode in this kind of exercise: discovering weeks in that the paper was never actually reproducible with the resources you have.

This lesson covers a concrete checklist for screening candidate papers before committing to one, why landmark heavily-cited papers are often worse reproduction targets than smaller specific ones, how to judge whether a paper's hardware requirements match what you can actually access, and a worked example screening three candidate papers against the checklist.

Before committing to a paper, check it against five things: does its circuit fit hardware or simulators you can actually access, like IBM Quantum's open tier or a local simulator; can you identify the exact circuit, parameters, and comparison from the text alone; is code or data actually available; is the scope realistic for your timeline, typically one figure or one table's main result, not the whole paper; and does later citing work give you independent context on whether the result is considered solid.

It's tempting to pick a famous, heavily-cited paper, but landmark results are frequently the hardest to reproduce precisely because they pushed the edge of available hardware at the time, often on access-restricted devices, with extensive supplementary engineering not fully described in the main text. A smaller, more specific, recent paper is usually a far better target: narrower scope, more current and accessible hardware, and often better-documented methodology precisely because it wasn't trying to be a landmark claim.

Screening three realistic candidates: a landmark fifty-plus-qubit quantum-advantage demonstration on a proprietary device with no code available is a reject on resource mismatch. A recent benchmark of two error-mitigation techniques on a three-qubit circuit on IBM's open-access hardware, with the circuit diagram and parameters given, is a strong candidate. A theoretical complexity-bound paper with no circuit implementation at all isn't an experimental reproduction target in the first place. The middle one is the realistic shape of a good capstone reproduction target.
Next lesson turns a chosen paper's prose, figures, and equations into a concrete, buildable plan — the exact circuit, parameters, and comparison — before you write a single line of code.
